question: How does Neeman make a continuous study in thirds change direction?
intro: Edward Neeman recorded the thirds étude for Musopen’s Set Chopin Free release. Compare its successive surges and withdrawals with Paderewski’s 1923 side rather than reducing either performance to one average speed.

cues.title: A modern recording release
cues.text: Neeman’s performance belongs to Musopen’s Set Chopin Free project. Compare the continuity of the paired upper notes with the lower line; no average-speed figure can describe every phrase.
cues.evidence: Commons identifies Neeman and the Musopen project. This is a general listening invitation, not a claim about the position of a particular third.

cues.title: The central contrast
cues.text: The sound changes noticeably through this central span while activity continues. Listen for a change of direction without assuming that a new colour requires a complete stop.
cues.evidence: The report’s strongest novelty boundary is 0:44; brightness rises to 927 Hz at 0:45 while attack density remains 3.8 per second. No chord or key is assigned from the machine estimate.

cues.title: A crest and withdrawal
cues.text: A strong later crest is followed by a marked reduction in recorded weight. Follow the connection across that withdrawal instead of judging the passage only by its busiest notes.
cues.evidence: The 1:25 window is the highest relative level, −5.8 dB; it falls to −16.2 at 1:30, where detected attacks drop to 2 per second.

cues.title: The ending opens out
cues.text: The last stretch separates its gestures more widely before the final resonance fades. Compare this closing space with Paderewski’s rather than treating the two file durations as identical playing times.
cues.evidence: A 1:56 novelty boundary accompanies low activity: 0.6 detected attacks per second at 1:55, 1 at 2:00 and none by 2:05. Full file duration is 130.2 seconds.

composer.born: 1 March 1810 by his family’s reckoning; the parish register gives 22 February, Żelazowa Wola, Duchy of Warsaw
composer.epithet: He made the piano sing through ornament, contrapuntal voice-leading and the unstable accents of Polish dance.
facts: Wojciech Żywny; Józef Elsner at Warsaw’s Main School of Music, 1826–29
Warsaw until 1830; Paris from 1831; summers at George Sand’s house in Nohant
Teaching, publication and selected performances, more often in salons than large public halls
Almost entirely centred on the piano: études, mazurkas, polonaises, nocturnes, preludes, ballades, scherzos, sonatas and concertos
composer.background:
Chopin was born at Żelazowa Wola in 1810, to a French-born father, Nicolas, and a Polish mother, Justyna Krzyżanowska. The family soon moved to Warsaw, where Nicolas taught French. The name Fryderyk belongs to his Polish life; Frédéric became usual in France. His family observed his birthday on 1 March, although the baptismal record gives 22 February. Piano lessons with Wojciech Żywny introduced Bach and Mozart alongside the fashionable repertory of the day. As a child he composed polonaises and played in aristocratic houses, but his later musical education extended beyond the cultivation of a prodigy.

Józef Elsner taught him harmony and composition at Warsaw’s Main School of Music from 1826 to 1829. Chopin heard Italian opera, encountered Polish vernacular music during visits outside the capital and learned the working forms of the virtuoso concerto. The F minor Concerto was composed before the E minor, despite their eventual numbering as Nos. 2 and 1. Both preserve an extended orchestral opening, but once the piano enters, its vocal line and ornament determine the movement’s scale. The slow movements belong as much to operatic singing as to the display repertory of a concert pianist.
